extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and legal practitioners handling patent equity/injunction cases
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules governing injunctions and appeals in patent suits in equity — including jurisdiction, form and content of injunctions, preliminary injunction practice (notice, affidavits, TROs, bonds), and appellate/certification procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appealability of certain interlocutory decrees (nominal complainant vs equitable owners)
rubrics_metrics.description: A decree by a court sustaining actions of a nominal complainant against the opposition of those equitably entitled to sue in the name of the nominal complainant is immediately appealable to the Circuit Court of Appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where members equitably entitled object to a nominal complainant's suit, the complainant may appeal immediately. (Case citations provided in text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial final/interlocutory decrees not appealable as final
rubrics_metrics.description: A decree sustaining part of the claims while dismissing another part is not appealable by the complainant as a final decree because it is interlocutory with respect to the sustained claims; the right to appeal is suspended until an accounting is had and a completely final decree disposing of the entire case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a decree is final only as to part of the claims but interlocutory as to others, the complainant must await a final decree disposing of the whole case before appealing as from a final decree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory decree awarding accounting only (patent expired) not appealable
rubrics_metrics.description: An interlocutory decree awarding merely an accounting and granting no injunction because the patent has expired is not appealable to the Circuit Court of Appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the patent expiration renders the injunction issue moot, such interlocutory decrees are not treated as appealable orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcript/stipulation rule for prosecuting appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution of an appeal includes procuring from the district court clerk a transcript of the record, or of such parts as the parties formally stipulate to be sufficient; the stipulation must be filed in the district court clerk's office and the clerk will prepare and certify the specified parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may agree by formal stipulation to limit the transcript to parts sufficient for the appellate decision; file the stipulation so the clerk can certify the transcript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible grounds for attacking or supporting a decree on appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: On appeal the decree may generally be attacked by the appellant on any ground upon which it was resisted in the court below; the appellee may support it on any ground in the record, whether relied on below or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellant's attack is generally confined to grounds raised below; appellee may assert additional record grounds. Non-jurisdictional and certain discretionary matters are exceptions (see other entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disallowance of appellate attack on discretionary rulings
rubrics_metrics.description: A decree cannot be assailed on appeal on grounds that are within the judicial discretion of the lower court (e.g., refusal to set aside a decree pro confesso, refusal to allow retraction of a pleading admission, granting/refusing rehearing, or other discretionary decisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discretionary procedural rulings are generally unreviewable on appeal; appellants should preserve exceptions below only where reviewable legal error exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master's accounting errors require exception below
rubrics_metrics.description: A decree cannot be attacked on the ground of an error made by a master in taking an account of profits or damages unless that error was brought before the court below for correction by a proper exception to the master's report; even then obvious quantity or computation errors only are reviewable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To preserve errors in a master's report for appeal, file proper exceptions and obtain correction in the court below; appellate relief is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Findings of fact by lower court generally respected on appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: When the court below has concurred with the master's findings of fact, those findings will not be disturbed by the appellate court except for strong reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts defer to trial fact-finding; only clear, strong reasons will justify reversal of findings of fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-review of prior errors on second appeal after remand
rubrics_metrics.description: When a decree is reversed and remanded and a second decree entered after further proceedings, that second decree cannot be assailed on account of errors that occurred prior to the former decree; and the decision of the appellate court on the first appeal is not reviewable on the second appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors corrected (or addressed) on the first appeal are not fresh grounds on subsequent appeals after remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellee cannot attack decree on appellant's appeal; separate appeal required to alter decree
rubrics_metrics.description: No decree can be attacked by the appellee on the appellant's appeal; a party who intends to ask the Circuit Court of Appeals to alter a decree must appeal to that tribunal whether the other party appeals or not. If both parties appeal, appeals are heard together, and the complainant below is entitled to open and close argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a party wants alteration, they must file their own appeal. Procedural posture matters for who may seek relief and how appeals are consolidated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments of error aimed at decree, not judge's reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments of error must be aimed at the decree of the court and not at the reasons which were stated by the judge for making that decree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On appeal focus on legal defects in the decree itself rather than mere judicial rationale; proper framing of assignments is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate outcomes and costs (affirm/reverse/modify/remand)
rubrics_metrics.description: After hearing, a Circuit Court of Appeals may affirm, reverse, modify, or remand. If it affirms on the merits it will generally affirm costs; if it reverses it generally does so at the appellee's costs. If it modifies the decree it may change the amount instead of remanding. If it remands, further proceedings are guided by the appellate decision as if originally rendered by the lower court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs follow typical appellate practice, with exceptions (e.g., absence of needed disclaimer may bar recovery of costs even on affirmance). If the appellate court omits costs, the lower court will normally not change its prior costs order on mandate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of division of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: A certificate of division of opinion (where two judges in the court below disagree) is a means of taking a question of law to the Circuit Court of Appeals; no question of infringement or other question of fact can be taken this way, and the certificate must state the precise points of law involved or the case will be remanded without an answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use certificate of division only for pure legal questions arising from multi-judge panels; ensure precise legal points are identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on appeals to the Supreme Court in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: No appeal may be taken to the Supreme Court from a final decree of the Court of Appeals of the District of Columbia which merely adjudges the validity or invalidity of a patent (such decrees may be reviewed by certiorari or certified questions). And no appeal lies from any Circuit Court of Appeals to the Supreme Court in any patent case except actions brought by the United States to repeal patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct appeals to the Supreme Court in patent litigation are tightly circumscribed; certiorari or statutory certification are the usual routes for Supreme Court review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification of pure questions of law to Supreme Court
rubrics_metrics.description: Any Circuit Court of Appeals may certify to the Supreme Court any pure question of law upon which it desires instruction; such a certificate must clearly and distinctly state the question and show that the appellate court desires the Supreme Court's instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certify only pure legal questions and clearly frame the issue and the request for instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court certiorari to Circuit Court of Appeals in patent equity cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court may send a writ of certiorari to any Circuit Court of Appeals requiring an action in equity for infringement to be sent to the Supreme Court for review; this power is exercised only in cases of great importance, conflicts among Circuits or with State courts, or questions affecting national interest, and lower courts will be reversed on questions of fact only when distinctly wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certiorari is exceptional and used sparingly for significant or conflicting questions; factual reversals require clear error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs when complainant succeeds on some patents or devices
rubrics_metrics.description: When in a suit on several patents the complainant succeeds on some and is defeated as to others, costs are in the discretion of the court and awarded according to the circumstances of the particular case. Likewise when the bill charges infringement by several devices and only one is proven to infringe. When an injunction is denied only because the patent has expired pendente lite the plaintiff is entitled to costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs are discretionary and depend on partial success or reason for denial (e.g., expiration pendente lite). Courts weigh circumstances in awarding costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction to grant injunctions in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction to grant injunctions to prevent violation of patent rights is conferred by statute upon the same courts that are vested with common-law jurisdiction in patent cases; the jurisdiction is to be exercised according to the course and principles of courts of equity and upon such terms as the court may deem reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable principles and the peculiar circumstances of patent rights inform the rules; some rules apply only to preliminary injunctions, some only to permanent injunctions, others to both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form requirements for injunctions (Clayton Act §19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every order of injunction or restraining order shall set forth the reasons for issuance, shall be specific in terms, and shall describe in reasonable detail (not by reference to the bill or other document) the act(s) sought to be restrained, and shall be binding only upon the parties to the suit, their officers, agents, servants, employees and attorneys, or those in active concert or participating with them who have received actual notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Injunctions must state reasons and be specific; do not attempt to bind unnamed or un-notified third parties; describe the prohibited acts in reasonable detail within the order itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and temporal scope of a preliminary injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: A preliminary injunction is one granted after filing the bill and before the case is ready to be decided on its prayer for a permanent injunction or for profits/damages. It is usually applied for before the answer but may be issued later; it may be dissolved at any time and, if not terminated earlier, continues until the interlocutory decree when it is dissolved or made permanent according to the equities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary injunctions are interlocutory and provisional; they may be dissolved or converted to permanent relief depending on subsequent proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of the bill vs affidavits for preliminary injunctions (Equity Rules effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Previously bills were required to state prior adjudication or acquiescence supporting presumptions of validity; under the present Equity Rules a bill is merely a statement of ultimate facts and allegations of prior adjudication/acquiescence are better presented in affidavits accompanying the motion. The bill must contain a specific prayer for an injunction pendente lite and conform to requisites of bills in equity (Equity Rule 25).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not plead evidentiary allegations as ultimate facts in the bill; reserve evidentiary claims (prior adjudication or public acquiescence) for the affidavits on the motion where they show probable eventual success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice requirement for motions for preliminary injunctions and restraining orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Due notice of a motion for a preliminary injunction must be served on the party sought to be enjoined before the motion will be heard. The Clayton Act restored the requirement of reasonable notice for preliminary injunctions and restraining orders, unless immediate and irreparable damage would ensue if the restraining order were not granted immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide reasonable notice to the adverse party for hearings on preliminary relief unless emergency circumstances justify immediate ex parte relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit practice on motions for preliminary injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions for preliminary injunctions are heard on ex parte affidavits. The complainant's affidavits must show all facts necessary to prima facie entitle him to such relief. The defendant's affidavits must state all facts upon which he bases his defense; if by traverse, no further affidavits are admitted, but if by confession and avoidance the complainant may reply with affidavits (no rejoinder allowed). Sworn bills/answers on file may be used as affidavits. Statements in the complainant's affidavits are taken as true if uncontradicted; defendant's affidavits are taken as true if consistent and not contradicted by reply. Affidavits ought to be served on opposite counsel a reasonable time before argument; late affidavits may be rejected or accepted with opportunity to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare thorough affidavits to establish prima facie case; anticipate traverse vs confession-and-avoidance responses; serve affidavits timely to avoid rejection or adjournment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension and withdrawal of motions for preliminary injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the complainant's moving papers lack a necessary point that can presumably be supplied, the court may suspend the motion to enable the complainant to supply it. The complainant may withdraw his motion at any time before decision, even over defendant's objection, without permanently relinquishing his contention. Procedural devices like demurrers or motions to dismiss may affect scheduling as formerly with demurrers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to supply missing points when a motion is suspended; withdrawal is available pre-decision but tactical consequences should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary restraining orders (TROs) and security requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A temporary restraining order may be made where danger of irreparable injury from delay appears and notice of a motion for a preliminary injunction has been given; since the Clayton Act, security must be required as a condition of granting either a restraining order or a temporary injunction. If defendant denies infringement since the beginning of the suit and asserts abandonment of infringement and non-recurrence, danger of irreparable injury is not shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TROs require a showing of immediate irreparable harm and (post-Clayton) a security bond; defendants' sworn abandonment can defeat TRO requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements required for prima facie preliminary injunction (two presumptions and one certainty)
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a prima facie case for a preliminary injunction the judge looks for two presumptions (validity of the patent and defendant's infringement) and one certainty (the complainant's title to the patent). If any of these is absent, no preliminary injunction will be granted except in unusual circumstances; if all are present and no good defense is interposed, or unless the court accepts a bond in lieu, a writ will generally be granted. A preliminary injunction will not be granted when defendant is responsible and a substantial doubt of infringement exists, or where the complainant's right is doubtful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish the patentee's title clearly and present strong prima facie proof of validity and infringement. If substantial doubt exists as to infringement or the patentee's right, preliminary relief is unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources and limits of the presumption of patent validity for preliminary relief
rubrics_metrics.description: A special presumption of validity exists where the patent has been suitably adjudicated in a Federal court, where its validity has been suitably acquiesced in by the public, where a decree pro confesso has been allowed, or where the defendant does not deny validity. The presumption does not arise merely from unattended letters patent. Prior adjudication gives a strong presumption, but a weak or unopposed prior defense may limit its effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on formal prior adjudication or clear public acquiescence to support the presumption of validity; beware that weak prior litigation may not strengthen the presumption.
